summary: Describes how RSVP PathErr messages can trigger rerouting of point-to-point MPLS and GMPLS traffic engineering label switched paths without first tearing down the path state or its resources. This enables smoother reroutes. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When a road needs to be moved, you can send a note asking drivers to switch to a new route without closing the old road first. This document describes that note for network paths.

subtitle: How a router asks the routers upstream to steer an MPLS or GMPLS path around it, without tearing the path down first.

tldr.problem: A node on an established MPLS or GMPLS path sometimes needs traffic moved away from itself or one of its resources, for example for soft-preemption or graceful shutdown, but the path should not be torn down first.
tldr.mechanism: The node sends an RSVP PathErr message upstream with a reroute error code. The ingress finds an alternate path and sets it up make-before-break. An optional timeout forces removal if nobody reacts.
tldr.outcome: The document reuses existing RSVP-TE mechanisms and adds one new error code, Reroute (34), for future reroute-specific error values. It applies to point-to-point LSPs only.

today: RFC 5710 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2010. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Reroute Requests Are Needed
sections.content:
RSVP, extended for traffic engineering by RFC 3209 (MPLS) and RFC 3473 (GMPLS), controls Label Switched Paths (LSPs). A PathErr message reports errors to nodes upstream of the node that detected the problem. Under RFC 2205, PathErr messages do not change path state in the nodes they pass through.

PathErr is mostly used while an LSP is being set up. This document covers a use after the LSP exists: a node tells an upstream node that it wants the LSP rerouted around the node itself or around resources tied to it. Soft-preemption (RFC 5712) and graceful shutdown are given as examples. The document calls such an indication a reroute request.

A reroute request can be issued without disrupting data traffic. When desired, a timeout can instead force removal of the LSP state and resources. Only point-to-point LSPs are covered; point-to-multipoint is left for further study.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a stop on a bus route needs to be skipped. The stop sends a message back along the route asking the bus company to pick a different way, without cancelling the bus.

sections.title: How a Reroute Request Is Signaled
sections.content:
The request travels from a downstream node (a transit or egress node) toward the ingress. It is carried in a PathErr message whose ERROR_SPEC object holds an error code and error value. The RFC says that the address and TLVs in the ERROR_SPEC identify the resource to avoid, not the error code and value.

A node that cannot act on the request itself MUST send a PathErr with one of three combinations:

  • Notify / Local node maintenance required, for backwards compatibility, to reroute around the local node.
  • Notify / Local link maintenance required, for backwards compatibility, to reroute around a local interface.
  • Reroute / any Reroute error value, for future compatibility when backwards compatibility is not a concern.

Everything else is handled with mechanisms from RFC 4920 (crankback) and RFC 4736 (reoptimization). The document only describes a sequence of actions using them.
sections.eli5: The note uses one of three standard phrases. The address written on the note tells everyone which place to avoid, not the phrase itself.

sections.title: What the Requesting Node Does
sections.content:
The node first checks whether it can act locally. The check MUST respect the Explicit Route Object (ERO) from the incoming Path message, which may rule out local rerouting. Any local repair SHOULD be done only if local policy allows it for that LSP.

If it cannot, it sends the PathErr described above. When rerouting around the local node, the local node MUST be named in the ERROR_SPEC. Otherwise the affected interface MUST be named, and the IF_ID ERROR_SPEC format SHOULD be used. A request more specific than an interface MUST use the IF_ID format, and TLVs may name a specific item such as a label.

Timeouts. If the node wants the LSP gone when nobody responds, it MUST start a reroute request timeout after sending. A PathTear, or a trigger Path message with an ERO avoiding the resource, cancels the timeout. So does normal refresh processing removing the Path state. If the timeout expires, the node MUST remove the LSP and its state and resources. It signals this downstream with PathTear and upstream with a PathErr carrying Service preempted, with the Path_State_Removed flag set if supported. Without that flag, it MUST also send a ResvTear.
sections.eli5: The sender first checks whether it can fix things itself. If not, it sends the note and starts a timer. If nobody changes the route before the timer rings, it closes the road for good.

sections.title: Upstream Nodes and the Ingress
sections.content:
A transit node whose policy supports reroute handling MUST examine incoming PathErr messages and MUST check for all three code combinations. It MAY act locally if the ERO does not preclude it, such as for loosely routed next hops, and SHOULD limit local repair attempts. The RFC expects policy to usually rule local repair out.

If the transit node supports RFC 4920, is a boundary node and boundary rerouting is allowed, it SHOULD use the request as a trigger. It MUST first find an alternate path within the domain, then terminate the PathErr and issue a new Path message. If it cannot act, it MUST propagate the PathErr to the previous hop.

The ingress MUST check received PathErr messages for reroute requests and MUST try to find an alternate path avoiding the named node, interface or resource. If none exists, the request MUST be discarded. If one exists, a make-before-break LSP SHOULD be initiated and standard make-before-break procedures MUST be followed.
sections.eli5: Each stop along the way either fixes the route itself or passes the note back. The starting point builds a new route first, and only then drops the old one.

sections.title: Example ERROR_SPEC Formats
sections.content:
This section is informative. A reroute request is always a PathErr, carrying either an RFC 2205 or an IF_ID (RFC 3473) ERROR_SPEC. Four examples show how to name what should be avoided.

  • Node: an IPv4 ERROR_SPEC (Class 6, C-Type 1) with the node address set to the local TE router address, and the error code Notify/Local node maintenance required or Reroute.
  • Interface: an IF_ID ERROR_SPEC (C-Type 3) with a TLV of Type 1 carrying the TE address of the interface to avoid.
  • Component: for an unnumbered component, per RFC 4201, a TLV of Type 3 carrying the router ID and the Interface ID assigned by the local node.
  • Label: per RFC 4920, the interface TLV (Type 1) plus a Type 6 TLV holding the DOWNSTREAM_LABEL to avoid.
sections.eli5: The note can say avoid this whole stop, avoid this one door, avoid this one lane inside it, or avoid this one ticket number.

sections.title: The New Reroute Error Code
sections.content: IANA assigned error code 34, named Reroute, in the RSVP Parameters registry. One error value is defined: 0, Generic LSP reroute request. Further values are allocated by IETF Consensus in the range 0 to 32767, and 32768 to 65535 is Private Use.
sections.eli5: The document asks for one new official label, number 34, so future special reasons for rerouting can be added under it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The text points to Section 9 of RFC 4920 and to RFC 4736 as the starting point. It says the new error code is functionally equivalent to the existing Notify local node and local link maintenance combinations. The document therefore introduces no new security considerations beyond those formats and mechanisms. Future documents defining new error values should discuss considerations specific to them.
sections.eli5: Because the new label means the same as ones already in use, it does not open any new doors for trouble.
